overview: The Sixteen Kingdoms were competing states across northern China during 304 to 439. Their rulers, soldiers, merchants and monks came from many backgrounds. This map combines them into one outline; its surviving 400 to 500 border interval outlasts the period, and it omits western communities discussed here.

periods.title: New courts after imperial breakdown
periods.summary: Liu Yuan proclaimed himself king of Han in 304, one starting point for the conventional Sixteen Kingdoms period.

periods.title: Courts, worship and workshops
periods.summary: A bronze Buddha inscribed in 338 provides a securely dated glimpse of Buddhist worship and skilled metalworking.

periods.title: Former Qin’s southern campaign fails
periods.summary: Eastern Jin defeated Fu Jian’s Former Qin army at the Fei River in 383; a bid to conquer the south failed.

periods.title: Translation and the last rival courts
periods.summary: Kumarajiva reached Later Qin’s Chang’an in 401. Northern Wei’s reunification of the north in 439 conventionally ends the period.

items.text: The number sixteen is a historical convention: historian Charles Holcombe counts as many as twenty-two significant states. Some were large, multiethnic conquest empires whose rulers claimed the title of emperor; others were independent governors who still professed loyalty to Jin. Sharing a map color did not mean sharing a government.

In 383, Former Qin ruler Fu Jian tried to conquer Eastern Jin in the south. His army was defeated at the Fei River near Bagongshan. The battle illustrates how quickly an ambitious court could lose its advantage. Eastern Jin was a separate southern state, not another name for the whole northern collection.

Helian Bobo’s Xia state built its capital at Tongwancheng, in present-day northern Shaanxi. Its remains include an outer city and two inner-city divisions, with the palace area in the west. Towers, projecting defenses, protected entrances and moats made this a carefully organized urban stronghold. A ruler associated with steppe peoples could also commission a substantial city.

What held Tongwancheng’s pale walls together? Researchers tested samples from the west city and identified lime, sand and clay, with organic additives including peach gum. Their experiments suggest that lime, light river clay and surface calcium carbonate helped produce the whiteness. The familiar “white city” nickname has a material story beneath it.

sections.title: Families, work and messages from far away

items.text: Around 313 to 314, a Sogdian woman named Miwnay wrote from Dunhuang to her mother Chatis. Abandoned by her husband, she lacked money and clothing and depended on a priest’s charity. In another letter, her daughter Shayn added her own account of tending animals. The surviving pages let a mother and child speak across sixteen centuries.

The same letter collection names pepper, musk, silver and cloth moving along trade routes. Merchants had to find partners, arrange transport and wait for news over enormous distances. One abandoned commercial partner had to return from Dunhuang to Guzang. Trade meant worried correspondence as well as valuable cargo.

A merchant’s letter to Samarkand reported famine and the burning of Luoyang in 311. He also complained that news from associates had stopped arriving. This is a contemporary report, with the writer’s own uncertainties: warfare appears through broken communication and concern for absent people, rather than only a list of victories.

At Leijiacun near Xianyang, excavators found miniature wells, granaries, stoves and mills in tombs, alongside pottery animals and carts. These objects supplied the deceased with an imagined household. Even in the afterlife, somebody apparently expected the grain to be stored and dinner to be prepared.

One Leijiacun burial contained piglet skulls; another had skulls above a stone covering a small pit of millet remains. Excavators interpreted these as funeral offerings. The grain survived as fragile pale husks, a reminder that food history can begin with something far less glamorous than a royal banquet.

Two bronze seals from Leijiacun carried military office titles. Together with twelve tombs arranged in two planned rows, they led excavators to suggest a military family cemetery. Names and biological relationships were not established by the report. The discovery connects army service with household objects and remembrance of relatives.

Four seated female musician figures from Pingling tomb M1 wear painted clothes and flat black headdresses. Three retain identifiable instruments: a zheng zither, a drum and a pipa lute. The fourth looks ready to blow an instrument, but that object is missing. Archaeology occasionally delivers the band with one instrument lost.

In the Xianyang and Xi’an area, many cemeteries used neat parallel rows, with tombs placed at regular intervals. Archaeologists identify these as planned family burial grounds. Remembering relatives involved organizing space as well as arranging ceremonies; a cemetery could preserve a family’s connections over successive burials.

A brick from Wenlin tomb M49 names a woman of the Zhang family as the wife of Zhu Yi and dates the burial to 378. Such a short inscription helps archaeologists compare and date other graves. An individual woman’s memorial becomes a chronological landmark for a much larger regional history.

Try reading a dated object: 建武四年 means “fourth year of the Jianwu reign era,” here 338. These characters open the surviving inscription on a gilded bronze Buddha from Later Zhao, now in San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. This is the museum’s transcription in standard Chinese characters, rather than a reproduction of the original letterforms.

A technical study found that the 338 Buddha was cast in sections of a clay mold fitted around a core, leaving space for molten bronze. Bronze spacers helped hold the arrangement. A gold surface finished the object; the mercury gilding used for it produced dangerous fumes. Religious splendor depended on demanding workshop labor.

The Buddha has clues to missing decorations: a projection behind its head probably held a halo, while holes on the base may once have supported a lotus and lions. Looking carefully turns an apparently complete museum statue into a small reconstruction puzzle.

Kumarajiva, a Buddhist scholar born in Kucha, reached Chang’an in 401 after years of captivity. Later Qin ruler Yao Xing commissioned translations of Buddhist scriptures into Chinese. Dozens of translations are attributed to him, helping establish major traditions of Chinese Buddhism. This influential exchange of learning took place amid coercion and warfare as well as royal support.

ending.text: Northern Wei reunited northern China in 439, the conventional endpoint of the Sixteen Kingdoms period. This ended the era of rival regional courts, not the lives of their inhabitants. Their cities, religious communities, crafts and family traditions form part of the history that followed.
